S0/C1 gave the largest unconstrained recovery observed (~0.494) but extreme fines (~0.987; runner-operation-0144). S3/C1 sacrifices some recovery but enables a qualitatively different particle regime.

**H2 [rejected as general control strategy]** For S2, larger seed charge, long holding, reheat/recool, and very slow staged cooling did not reduce fines below ~0.98 (runner-operation-0051, -0059, -0079, -0082, -0092 through -0105). These variables cannot be assumed transferable across solvents.

**H3 [supported, narrow process window]** With S3/C1, cooling only to 300 K gave fines ~0.756 (runner-operation-0225), whereas continued cooling to 250 K followed by twelve 4 h low-temperature holds produced purity ~0.976, fines ~0.388, and seed-excluded recovery ~0.427 (runner-operation-0241). The effect is associated with the combined deeper cooling plus long hold; those factors were not separated.

**H4 [supported catalyst specificity]** Repeating the deep-cool/long-hold S3 workup with C0, C2, or C3 did not reproduce compliant fines (all ~0.675–0.693; runner-operation-0265, -0289, -0313). Thus C1 is required within the tested catalyst set, despite C0 giving a numerically higher recovery than C1 under that workup.

**Decision.** Recommend batch 9: it is the only observed batch satisfying both purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50, and its recovery (~0.427) substantially exceeds the initial feasibility target. Key unresolved question is whether the 250 K endpoint or the 48 h hold is the dominant cause; either change could invalidate compliance.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Solvent S2 should favor larger, purer crystals and fewer fines because its nominal growth is high and nucleation/occlusion low, but its low solubility may improve recovery. Catalyst C1 is the initial reaction prior because its nominal activity is highest. A moderate hot reaction followed by seeded slow cooling and a low-temperature hold should therefore give feasible recovery with purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50.

**Pre-experiment test:** Batch 1 will use full reagent/catalyst loading in S2, react hot, then seed and cool slowly. If conversion or recovery is poor, vary catalyst/temperature; if fines fail, reduce seed dose and/or slow cooling/extend growth hold. Material dossier is only a prior and may be misindexed.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in scope]
S2 consistently permits very high crystal purity after filtration. Single 14,400 s cooling to 275 K can satisfy fines, but repeating the cold stage can increase recovery while producing excessive fines (B2/B3 final assays: runner-operation-0027, runner-operation-0039). Thus recovery/fines tradeoff is dominated by thermal history rather than purity in this region.

## H2 [supported in scope]
C2 is inferior for target formation under 340 K/1800 s (HPLC runner-operation-0045) versus C0/C1/C3 screens. C1 and C3 are leading reaction catalysts; C1 at 340 K/1800 s had about 0.61 selectivity (runner-operation-0021), while overly severe C1 at 360 K/3600 s reached full conversion but more byproduct (runner-operation-0007).

## H3 [unresolved]
Batch-to-batch fines differ substantially even with nominally similar single-stage 275 K cooling (runner-operation-0015, -0050, -0061). Upstream impurity profile, catalyst identity, and seed effectiveness are confounded. Prediction: a larger seed dose and slightly warmer endpoint should reduce fines, though possibly at recovery cost.

**Decision:** retain S2, focus on C1/C3 with less severe reaction and single controlled cooling. Avoid repeated cold stages unless a later intervention demonstrably controls fines.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
S2 gives excellent filtered crystal purity across all completed conditions. Crystal recovery and fines are jointly governed by upstream target/impurity composition and crystallization supersaturation.

## H2 [supported in tested scope]
C1 at 350 K for 1800 s followed by 0.02 g seed and one 14,400 s cooling stage is the best observed feasible window. B10 at 275 K and B11 at 270 K both met purity/fines constraints and gave crystal_yield about 0.560 (runner-operation-0117, runner-operation-0128). The endpoint difference is numerically small relative to assay noise and run variability, so an endpoint effect is unresolved.

## H3 [supported]
Very high upstream target formation under 340 K/900 s did not translate into compliant solids at tested endpoints (B6-B9); fines stayed above 0.58. Conversely, severe 360 K/3600 s lowered selectivity but produced a feasible B1. This supports an impurity/supersaturation-mediated fines tradeoff rather than maximizing reaction yield alone.

## H4 [rejected in tested scope]
Increasing seed from 0.02 g to 0.05 g did not suppress fines (runner-operation-0072), and 0.005 g also failed (runner-operation-0080/-0086). A 300 K reheat/recool cycle did not improve the particle distribution (runner-operation-0083).

**Final test prediction:** repeating the 350 K/1800 s upstream window with a 265 K endpoint may slightly raise recovery while remaining near the fines limit. If fines exceed 0.50, prefer B10/B11 rather than the colder endpoint.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
S2 with C1 provides a robust high-purity route. The best observed upstream window was 0.04 mol reagent, 0.08 L S2, 0.005 mol C1, heated at 350 K for 1800 s with 500 rpm stirring.

## H2 [supported in tested scope]
With that upstream window, 0.02 g seed and one 14,400 s cooling stage over 275–265 K repeatedly met purity and fines specifications (B10–B12, runner-operation-0117, -0128, -0139). Colder endpoint differences are small and confounded with run variability, but B12 at 265 K had the highest observed compliant crystal_yield (0.571), purity 0.995, and fines 0.424.

## H3 [supported]
Maximizing liquid-phase target yield alone is not sufficient: 340 K/900 s produced higher-selectivity reaction mixtures but excessive fines in the tested crystallizations. Repeated cold stages increased fines, and a reheat/recool intervention did not rescue the distribution.

## Decision
Recommend completed Batch 12. It maximizes observed seed-excluded crystal recovery among batches satisfying purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50. B10/B11 independently support the same process window, though exact endpoint ranking remains unresolved within assay/process variability.

# Hypothesis notebook

## Prior expectations (before batch 1)
**H1 [tentative].** Because identities are opaque, catalyst/solvent choice and reaction temperature may dominate target formation. A broad categorical screen is warranted before local optimization.

**H2 [tentative].** For crystallization, seeding before a controlled slow cool and a low-temperature hold should reduce fines relative to an abrupt unseeded cool, while adequate reaction conversion and low-temperature residence should improve seed-excluded recovery. This may fail if the selected solvent retains product or if seed-induced nucleation creates many fines.

**Decision.** Use early batches to span catalyst/solvent and reaction temperature, with particle-size measurements on each batch when possible; then exploit the best spec-feasible region. A result would change this plan if no crystals or inadequate purity are observed.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only for reaction/recovery ranking]
Within the tested recipes, C0/S0 near 370 K gave the strongest combination of target formation and seed-excluded crystal recovery. Batch 1 returned crystal yield 0.4855 and purity 0.9876 (runner-operation-0015), numerically the highest observed recovery. Related C0/S0 variants remained near 0.44–0.48 recovery (runner-operation-0070, runner-operation-0206, runner-operation-0233). Categorical and thermal changes were confounded in some comparisons, so this is a local process conclusion rather than a material main-effect estimate.

## H2 [rejected in the explored scope]
The prior expectation that seeding plus slow cooling/holding would bring fines below 0.50 was not supported. Small seed, repeated seed addition, no seed, long low-temperature holds, staged cooling, thermal cycling, and one resuspension/recrystallization all gave final fines about 0.99–1.00 (final-assay evidence runner-operation-0015, -0038, -0051, -0070, -0124, -0139, -0160, -0173, -0187, -0206, -0220, -0233). Particle-size readings before filtration agreed qualitatively (e.g. runner-operation-0012, -0035, -0048, -0067, -0121, -0136, -0149, -0170, -0184, -0203, -0217). Thus the campaign found no spec-feasible batch.

## H3 [unresolved]
Fines appear insensitive to the tested seed dose, solvent volume, endpoint temperature, and residence histories, but those factors were not independently replicated and measurement uncertainty plus recipe confounding prevent claiming zero effect. The consistently narrow outcome range suggests an untested control or crystallization regime may be required. A future test should alter growth/nucleation conditions orthogonally rather than repeat the tested cool-and-hold patterns.

## Final decision
Recommend batch 1 because it has the highest observed seed-excluded crystal recovery while meeting the purity constraint. It fails the fines constraint (0.9973), so the recommendation is explicitly the best non-feasible result, not a compliant process.

# Pre-experiment hypotheses

**H1 [tentative]** Within the anonymous-material scope, S2 should favor recovery and coarse, low-fines crystals because its nominal solubility and nucleation tendency are lowest while growth is highest; its low occlusion should also support purity. S1 is the conservative comparator. This prior may be wrong or misindexed.

**H2 [tentative]** C1 or C2 at moderate loading and elevated reaction temperature should outperform C0; excessive temperature/time may reduce purity via byproduct/degradation. Initial screen will vary catalyst/solvent and reaction severity.

**H3 [tentative]** Slow cooling with modest seeding, followed by a cold hold, should reduce fines relative to rapid cooling; seed-excluded recovery may benefit from low final temperature and sufficient hold. A reheating/recooling history could ripen crystals but might sacrifice recovery.

Planned decision: use early final assays plus selected HPLC/particle measurements to locate a feasible recipe, then refine recovery while retaining purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50. Numerical differences will remain provisional without repeats.

# Working hypotheses after seven completed batches

**H1 [revised; supported for tested conditions]** Solvent controls the recovery–fines tradeoff more strongly than catalyst in the 365 K/3600 s, 0.04 mol reagent/0.055 L solvent regime. S1 gave the best observed compliant recovery (batch 6: crystal yield about 0.486, purity about 0.999, fines about 0.451; event runner-operation-0073). S0 increased reaction/crystal yield (batch 5: about 0.610/0.524) but failed fines (about 0.679; runner-operation-0061). S2 was cleaner/coarser but lower recovery (batches 1–4); S3 was borderline on fines and lower recovery (batch 7; runner-operation-0085). These are single-batch comparisons, so noise and uncontrolled run residuals remain alternatives.

**H2 [narrowed]** C2 is disfavored under the common S2 recipe; C0, C1, and C3 gave closer results, with C3 having the highest observed crystal yield (batch 4, runner-operation-0049). Differences between C0/C1/C3 are not yet repeat-confirmed. Use C3 provisionally.

**H3 [supported in direction, unresolved magnitude]** Relative to batch 1, colder/longer cooling with 0.05 g seed in batches 2–4 coincided with lower fines and larger size, but catalyst and stochastic effects confound the comparison. S1 with this schedule passed both constraints.

**Next predictions (pre-experiment):** A crystallization heat-cycle in S0 may ripen the fines enough to approach the <=0.50 constraint while retaining its higher reaction yield. For S1, reducing reaction severity may lower degradation/byproduct and could raise selective yield, while increased concentration may raise recovery but risks fines. I will test these separately; a failed S0 cycle would favor S1 refinement.

# Final source-stage interpretation

**H1 [supported in tested scope]** The solvent composition produced the clearest recovery–fines tradeoff. Pure S0 raised recovery but repeatedly failed the fines constraint (batches 5 and 8; runner-operation-0061 and runner-operation-0099). Pure S1 was compliant with lower recovery (batch 6; runner-operation-0073). A 20% S0 / 80% S1 volume blend combined higher recovery with a substantial fines margin in two independent completed batches (10 and 12; runner-operation-0124 and runner-operation-0149).

**H2 [supported provisionally]** For the blend recipe, observed crystal yields were about 0.501 and 0.495, with purities about 0.977 and 0.993 and fines about 0.451 and 0.441. Replication supports feasibility, though the small yield difference is within assay-scale variability and is not evidence that batch 10 is intrinsically better.

**H3 [rejected for tested cycle]** The S0 270 K cool / 300 K reheat / 250 K recool cycle did not control fines; batch 8 had about 0.805 fines despite high recovery (runner-operation-0099). Do not generalize this rejection beyond that exact thermal cycle.

**H4 [unresolved]** The 30% S0 blend also complied (batch 11; runner-operation-0137) but did not exceed the observed recovery of the 20% blend. With only one 30% run and assay noise, the optimum blend fraction remains unresolved.

**Decision:** Recommend completed batch 10 because it has the highest observed seed-excluded crystal recovery among batches meeting purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50: yield about 0.5008, purity about 0.9766, fines about 0.4508. Batch 12 is a reassuring exact-recipe replicate. Conditions: 0.04 mol reagent, 0.011 L S0 + 0.044 L S1, 0.004 mol C3; nitrogen control, 365 K for 3600 s at 600 rpm; 0.05 g seed; cool to 250 K over/for 14400 s; filter. This recommendation would change if repeat data established a higher compliant recovery for the 30% blend or another catalyst/thermal schedule.

versions.text:
# Initial hypotheses

**H1 [tentative].** Solvent S2 should favor high recovery and acceptable purity/fines because its nominal solubility and nucleation tendency are low while growth is high and occlusion low. Slow seeded cooling after a productive reaction should outperform abrupt unseeded cooling in particle size/fines. This may fail if fixed-world residuals reverse the dossier ranking.

**H2 [tentative].** Catalyst C1 is the best initial reaction choice from nominal activity; moderate temperature/time should raise conversion without excessive degradation. I will screen material choices and thermal histories, then replicate/refine promising conditions. A final result meeting purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50 will be prioritized by crystal_yield.

# Working hypotheses

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Catalyst and solvent identities will materially affect target formation, so an initial material screen should precede thermal-history optimization. I expect hotter reaction holds to raise conversion but very long/hot exposure may increase byproduct or degradation.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
For a productive reaction, seeded slow cooling followed by a cold hold should improve recovery and reduce fines versus abrupt unseeded cooling. A moderate seed dose should mainly control nucleation; because reported recovery excludes seed, excessive seed is not intrinsically beneficial.

**Planned falsification:** use early batches to screen catalyst/solvent combinations under a common reaction and crystallization protocol, then perturb cooling/hold and loading around the best feasible condition. I will prioritize assay-qualified recovery (purity >=0.80, fines <=0.50), not the native composite score.

# Working hypotheses

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
Material identity matters, but solvent choice has had the clearest particle-quality consequence under the common 360 K reaction and seeded cooling protocol. S0 batches remained extremely fine (final-assay fines 0.945–1.00 in events runner-operation-0015, -0028, -0046, -0059). With C1 and otherwise comparable crystallization, S1, S2, and S3 reduced fines to 0.588, 0.504, and 0.696 respectively (runner-operation-0072, -0085, -0098). These are numerical contrasts with multiple simultaneous solvent-specific reaction/solubility effects; they do not isolate mechanism.

## H2 [supported in S2/C1 scope]
Stopping seeded S2 crystallization warmer improved particle acceptability without a clear recovery penalty: 290 K gave crystal yield 0.413, purity 0.981, and fines 0.471 (runner-operation-0111), versus 285 K yield 0.414, purity 1.000, and fines 0.504 (runner-operation-0085). The fines shift exceeds either instrument's stated single-measurement noise scale, but repeatability is not yet established. Prediction: 288–290 K should remain near the fines limit and may maximize qualified recovery.

## H3 [revised / unresolved]
The initial general claim that more seeding and longer/cycled growth necessarily reduce fines is not supported. S0 remained fine across seed doses and a prolonged thermal cycle (runner-operation-0015 through -0059), and extended 295 K processing in batch 3 did not improve the final distribution (runner-operation-0046). Solvent-dependent nucleation/solubility is an alternative explanation. I will now optimize near S2/C1 and treat fines <=0.50 as the binding stopping criterion.

**Decision:** batch 8 is the first assay-qualified result. Remaining batches will test a slightly colder stop, catalyst choice, and seed/thermal-history robustness; I will retain batch 8 unless another completed batch has higher recovery while meeting both constraints.

# Final source-stage notebook

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
S2 with C1 and a 288–290 K stopping window produced the only robust cluster of assay-qualified outcomes. Batches 8, 10, and 11 all met purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50 (runner-operation-0111, -0137, -0150), with seed-excluded crystal recoveries 0.413, 0.410, and 0.396. Batch 9 with C0 also just met the constraints but had lower recovery, 0.390 (runner-operation-0124). Thus C1 is preferred over C0 in S2 under this protocol, while the exact size of that catalyst effect remains confounded by batch variation.

## H2 [supported, bounded]
The final crystallization stop is a binding trade-off. At 285 K with C1/S2, recovery was 0.414 but fines were 0.504, narrowly failing (runner-operation-0085). At 288–290 K, recoveries were similar within assay noise while fines were 0.471–0.496 in three qualified batches (runner-operation-0111, -0137, -0150). This supports stopping near 290 K rather than continuing colder growth. Exact temperature ranking is unresolved because recovery differences are on the order of the reported assay noise and exact 290 K replication differed numerically.

## H3 [rejected in tested form]
Lowering the reaction temperature to 350 K while extending the hold to 5400 s did not preserve recovery: batch 12 gave recovery 0.320 with higher byproduct/degradation signals, despite acceptable purity and fines (runner-operation-0162). The combined temperature-duration perturbation is confounded, so it does not isolate a temperature effect; nevertheless this recipe is not preferred.

## Final decision
Select lifecycle batch 8 (runner-operation-0111): crystal yield 0.413, purity 0.981, fines 0.471. It has the highest observed recovery among batches that satisfy both explicit quality constraints. Batch 6 had a numerically similar recovery (0.414) but failed the fines constraint, and later qualified repeats did not exceed batch 8.

# Working hypotheses

H1 [tentative] Solvent S2 should favor recovery and coarse, clean crystals because its dossier combines low relative solubility, high growth, low nucleation and low impurity occlusion. S1 is the conservative comparator; S0 is expected to give more fines/occlusion.

H2 [tentative] Catalyst C1 or C3 may outperform C0, but world-specific residuals could reverse the nominal ranking. A moderate-temperature reaction followed by controlled seeded cooling should preserve purity better than aggressive heat or crash cooling.

Prediction for batch 1: C1/S2 with near-full charge, moderate heating, seeding, slow cooling and growth hold will exceed the 0.10 recovery feasibility target while meeting purity >=0.80 and fines <=0.50. If reaction conversion is weak, test catalyst/temperature before refining crystallization; if fines are high, reduce seed and slow/interrupt cooling.

# Working hypotheses

H1 [supported in tested scope] S2 permits clean product: all four S2 batches met purity and fines constraints, with final crystal yields 0.35-0.42 (events runner-operation-0012, -0024, -0036, -0048). This is far above the feasibility target. Crystals remain small and fines are near the upper bound, so crystallization history still merits optimization.

H2 [tentative, revised] At 355 K/3600 s, C0 is the leading catalyst (batch 2, yield 0.417) but its numerical advantage over C3 (0.408) and C1 (0.388) is not yet repeatability evidence; C2 was poorer (0.350). HPLC selectivity/yield rankings broadly agree that C2 is weak, while C0/C1/C3 are close (events runner-operation-0007, -0019, -0031, -0043).

Next tests: use C0/S2 to map reaction temperature, then compare solvents. Prediction: lower reaction temperature may reduce byproduct but risk incomplete conversion; S1 may improve purity but lower recovery, while S3 may improve upstream formation but worsen crystallization quality. After identifying a reaction regime, test deeper/slower cooling and growth holds to raise recovery without pushing fines above 0.50.

# Working hypotheses

H1 [supported in tested scope] Reaction temperature dominates the tested upstream conditions: C0/S2 at 375 K for 2400 s produced 0.524 crystal yield with acceptable purity/fines (batch 6, runner-operation-0072), versus 0.417 at 355 K (batch 2) and 0.291 at 335 K (batch 5). HPLC selectivity increased correspondingly (runner-operation-0055, -0067). The tested safety risk remained below the campaign limit.

H2 [supported qualitatively] S2 is preferable downstream. S1 at 355 K gave similar high yield but fines 0.550 (batch 7), and S3 produced fines 0.793 (batch 8); both violated the fines constraint. This solvent comparison is confounded by temperature relative to the selected 375 K regime, so it supports but does not prove an intrinsic solvent effect.

H3 [tentative] With C0/S2 at 375 K, low seed dose and staged slow cooling should modestly improve recovery while retaining fines compliance. Batch 9 used 0.005 g seed and staged cooling to 278 K and reached yield 0.527, purity 0.985, fines 0.452 (runner-operation-0109); the numerical gain over batch 6 is small relative to unknown run variability. Test deeper cooling plus a growth/ripening hold; abandon deeper cooling if fines cross 0.50.

# Final source-stage hypotheses

H1 [supported in sampled domain] For C0/S2 with the tested loading, hotter short reaction treatments improved overall crystal recovery and reaction selectivity without violating purity or fines constraints: 375 K gave 0.544 yield after deep staged cooling/hold (batch 10, runner-operation-0123), 395 K gave 0.592 (batch 11, runner-operation-0137), and 415 K gave 0.626 (batch 12, runner-operation-0151). The upward differences are numerically larger than adjacent instrument noise, but temperature and duration changed together and each condition lacks replication, so the precise causal law and optimum remain unresolved.

H2 [supported in sampled domain] Staged cooling to 265 K followed by a low-agitation hold retained fines compliance while increasing recovery relative to the earlier 278 K recipes. Batch 10 reached fines 0.435 and yield 0.544 versus batch 9 at fines 0.452 and yield 0.527 (events runner-operation-0123 and -0109). This comparison is not a clean decomposition because the final temperature and hold both changed.

H3 [supported for decision] Batch 12 is the best observed feasible process: crystal yield 0.626, purity 0.999, fines 0.468, with crystal size index 0.099 and CSD quality 0.661 (runner-operation-0151). Batch 11 provides a more comfortable fines margin (0.431) but lower yield (0.592). Since the research goal prioritizes maximum recovery subject to the stated constraints, select batch 12.

Scope and unresolved alternatives: the campaign did not replicate the leading condition, independently separate reaction temperature from residence time, or test beyond 415 K. The batch-12 fines result is close enough to the 0.50 limit that confirmation would be prudent. A future result showing reproducible fines above 0.50 or lower recovery would favor batch 11; otherwise extend the temperature/residence-time map cautiously and refine the 265 K hold.

# Pre-experimental hypotheses

**H1 [tentative].** Solvent S2 should favor the specification because its nominal low solubility and nucleation tendency plus high growth imply stronger recovery with fewer/larger particles; S3 is the conservative alternative. This may be overturned by fixed-world residuals.

**H2 [tentative].** Catalyst C1 is the initial reaction-screen choice from nominal activity. At fixed charge, adequate hot residence should increase conversion, while excessive temperature/time may raise degradation. A first batch at moderate-high temperature will test feasibility.

**H3 [tentative].** Slow cooling, modest seeding, and a cold hold should reduce fines compared with unseeded/fast cooling. Particle sizing will be used selectively to distinguish thermal-history effects.

# Working hypotheses after batches 1–5

**H1 [supported in tested scope].** S2 supports high-purity crystal recovery: all five S2 batches gave final purity about 0.98–1.00. Batch 2–5 slow 14,400 s cooling to 270 K also reduced fines to about 0.32–0.34, unlike batch 1's shorter cooling plus ambient-warming hold (fines 0.527). Thermal history is confounded with reaction conditions in batch 1, so the cooling interpretation remains provisional.

**H2 [supported for 360 K/1800 s, S2].** Catalyst C3 gave the highest observed final crystal yield (0.528, event runner-operation-0041) among C0/C1/C2/C3 under the matched recipe; C0 0.502, C1 0.484, C2 0.413. Single runs and assay noise mean modest C3–C0 differences are not yet repeatability evidence, but C3 is the optimization choice.

**H3 [revised].** 380 K/3600 s is unnecessarily severe: batch 1 had degradation warning 0.243 and lower final yield than moderate 360 K/1800 s batches. Moderate conditions retained near-complete conversion and improved selectivity. Next: screen solvent identity at fixed C3, then optimize seeding/cold endpoint around S2/C3.

# Final source-stage synthesis

**H1 [supported in this campaign].** Solvent identity strongly affected the recovery–fines tradeoff at matched C3/360 K/1800 s/270 K cooling. S1 gave 0.605 crystal yield with fines 0.346 (runner-operation-0071), whereas S0 gave higher reaction yield but fines 0.755 and S3 fines 0.694 (runner-operation-0061, -0081). S2 was feasible but lower crystal recovery (best 0.528 in the matched catalyst screen, runner-operation-0041).

**H2 [supported in tested scope].** C3 was the best catalyst choice in the S2 matched screen; the C3–C0 margin is modest and unreplicated, but later S1/C3 runs repeatedly met purity and fines constraints.

**H3 [supported with uncertainty].** Lowering the S1 crystallization endpoint from 270 to 250 K increased observed recovery from roughly 0.60 to 0.62–0.63 while retaining fines below 0.50 (runner-operation-0101, -0111). Seed 0.01 versus 0.05 g did not show a resolved effect relative to assay/particle uncertainty. The 0.04 L concentrated batch reached 0.633 yield but fines 0.487 (runner-operation-0121), too close to the 0.50 limit given stated 0.018 assay noise.

**Decision.** Recommend batch 10 rather than batch 12: batch 10 has essentially the same recovery within measurement resolution (0.630 vs 0.633) but a more defensible fines margin (0.433 vs 0.487), with purity 0.981. This decision would change if replicated concentrated batches demonstrate underlying fines safely below 0.50 without sacrificing recovery.

# Working hypotheses

H1 [tentative] Reaction conversion/selectivity will depend strongly on anonymous catalyst, temperature, and time. Initial screen will compare catalysts under a common moderate-hot reaction; HPLC will distinguish productive conditions.

H2 [tentative] Slow cooling with a modest seed dose followed by a cold hold should reduce fines relative to unseeded/fast cooling while preserving recovery. Greater reagent loading and colder endpoint should raise overall crystal recovery, potentially trading against purity or fines.

Decision: screen broadly first, then spend later batches refining the best feasible process. These claims would change if early assays show weak catalyst effects or no crystallization.

# Working hypotheses

H1 [supported in screened scope] Catalyst/solvent and thermal history materially affect reaction and crystallization outcomes. Under C0, 360 K/1800 s, the solvent screen gave large morphology differences: S0 remained overwhelmingly fine (batches 1 and 3), S1 was near the fines boundary with higher recovery (batch 4), S2 met both constraints with somewhat lower recovery (batch 5), and S3 produced excessive fines (batch 6). These are numerical single-batch comparisons; replication is still needed.

H2 [revised] A 0.05 g seed plus slow cooling alone is not generally enough to suppress fines; solvent identity is dominant in the tested recipes. For S1, slightly warmer endpoints, longer ripening, or mild thermal cycling should plausibly move fines below 0.50 while retaining much of the observed ~0.53 recovery. For S2, colder operation may raise recovery while preserving the observed fines margin.

Decision: focus remaining batches on S1/S2 boundary optimization and replication. Prefer feasible final-assay results over particle-size snapshots when selecting because the required endpoint is the destructive final assay. Suspend broad catalyst screening unless refined crystallization loses feasibility.

# Final working interpretation

H1 [supported in tested scope] Solvent identity dominates morphology for the common C0 reaction and slow-cooling protocol. S0 and S3 gave excessive fines; S1 remained near or above the 0.50 limit despite warmer endpoints and one mild thermal cycle (batches 4, 7, 8). S2 produced feasible solids across batches 5 and 9–12.

H2 [supported in tested S2 scope] Lowering the S2 crystallization endpoint from 290 K to 280, 270, and 250 K increased observed overall recovery while final fines stayed below 0.50 (batches 5, 9, 10, 11). Because these are not exact replicates and final-assay noise/process variability are present, the trend is useful but not a precision law.

H3 [tentative] Raising concentration from 0.04 mol/0.08 L to 0.04 mol/0.06 L at the 250 K endpoint further improved recovery and size without violating purity/fines constraints (batch 12 versus batch 11), but this single comparison is confounded by run-to-run variability.

Decision: recommend batch 12. It has the highest observed feasible crystal_yield (~0.554), with crystal_purity ~0.997 and fines ~0.414. Batch 11 is a nearby, lower-loading feasible fallback (~0.547 yield, ~0.992 purity, ~0.372 fines) if a larger fines margin is prioritized. Claims are confined to anonymous benchmark materials and the tested operating window.
